citation: Papenfuss, T., Shafiei Bafti, S. & Sharifi, M. 2021. Eublepharis macularius. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2021: e.T164745A1072324. Accessed on 15 May 2026.

actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: This South Asian species ranges from south of the Hindu Kush (Afghanistan) and Northwest Frontier Province (Pakistan), through Pakistan south to Rajputana and the Khandesh District of western India (Anderson 1999). There is an early 1900s record of a gecko tentatively assigned to this taxon from Khorasan in Iran, near the Afghan border, but the specimens were lost before they could be deposited and the presence of the species in Iran remains uncertain (Anderson 1999). It is widespread within most of its range, however, there appears to be a disjunct subpopulation in eastern Afghanistan (Sindaco and Jeremčenko 2008). This may be an artefact of limited surveying in the Registan Desert area. A recent record from the Kamdi Biological Corridor represents the first record from Nepal (Rawat et al. 2019); these authors also reported photographic evidence of the species' occurrence in a village in Nawalparasi District and in school grounds in Gurvakot in Surkhet District. The Nepalese records represent a range of extension of around 500 km to the east of the closest known Indian locality (Rawat et al. 2019). It occurs up to around 2,500 m asl (Szczerbak and Golubev 1996).
documentation.population: In Iran, this species is known only from a single tentative record. It is common in stony habitats in Pakistan (Khan 2006). Its distribution and abundance in Afghanistan are uncertain due to limited recent sampling: Wagner et al. (2016) report five localities, each represented by one or two specimens.
documentation.habitats: This is a nocturnal and terrestrial species. In Afghanistan, it has been found on fairly open alluvial soil (Anderson 1999). In Pakistan, it has been recorded in rocky desert and sparse grassland with clay, and crevices in rock walls (Minton 1966, Anderson 1999), and colonies appear to exhibit a preference for stone boundary walls around fields or houses (Khan 2006). The Kamdi record was of two males found hibernating in a dead tree in mixed hardwood forest, a more mesic and densely-vegetated habitat than other known localities which nonetheless represents the driest montane habitat in Nepal (Rawat et al. 2019). The species lives in colonies (Minton 1966), and it can be found in large numbers on warm, humid nights in the wet season (Khan 2006). It hibernates between October and February in much of its range, but may be active into November in warmer areas (Khan 2006). The female lays several clutches of one or two eggs; in captivity animals have been recorded laying four clutches with a four week interval over a year (Szczerbak and Golubev 1996). Eggs take approximately a month to hatch (Khan 2006).
documentation.threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species as a whole. This species breeds regularly in captivity and is common in the international pet trade, however both legal and illegal collection from the wild are ongoing (Mirza et al. 2014). Animals are frequently confiscated at the Nepal-India border; while these have been thought to originate in India at least some of these animals may represent offtake from recently-identified Nepalese subpopulations (Rawat et al. 2019). The Kambi subpopulation is known from forest where logging has been observed, while one of the other Nepalese records was taken during gravel extraction (Rawat et al. 2019).
documentation.measures: It is presumably present in a number of protected areas within its range. Further studies are needed to determine if this species is present in extreme southeastern Iran, and in future to clarify the extent of its distribution in Afghanistan. Taxonomic clarification of the validity of Eublepharus afghanicus is recommended.
documentation.use_trade: The leopard gecko is extremely common in the international pet trade, and is widely bred in captivity. It may be that most animals found in the pet trade are now captive-bred. It is consequently unclear whether wild-caught animals are still entering the pet trade in significant numbers (although collection from the wild is ongoing - Mirza et al. 2014), and Pakistan has strict permitting requirements for export. Local communities in Pakistan include traditional collectors of this species, suggesting that there remain economic incentives for harvesting this species.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Eublepharis macularius fuscus has been elevated to specific status (Das 1997), but the validity of several proposed subspecies and their status is unclear (discussed in (Sindaco and Jeremčenko 2008, Khan 2006 and Wagner et al. 2016). This assessment follows Wagner et al. (2016) in treating the proposed species E. gracilis, described from a captive specimen of unknown origindescribed from a captive specimen of unknown origin, as a nomen dubium. These authors propose recognizing E. m. afghanicus as a full species but note that this status needs to be verified. On this basis, E. afghanicus is tentatively retained within the synonym of E. macularius in this assessment
